contributions: A dataset of 6,728 filtered DeepSeek-R1 reasoning traces with ranking labels for listwise table reranking on NQ-Tables, released with code and models

CoTCond, a conditional reasoning distillation objective that places the teacher trace in the input and computes loss only over the ranking, contrasted against CoTGen trace imitation and reasoning-free Naive SFT under identical LoRA settings
Out-of-distribution evaluation on four Multi-Table QA Benchmark subsets showing CoTCond best on every metric, including the financial-domain TAT-QA shift
An error decomposition attributing most of the reasoning-distillation gain to eliminating parse failures, empty outputs and duplicate predictions rather than to finer ranking order
datasets: Multi-Table QA Benchmark subsets: HybridQA (6,106 queries / 17,229 tables), SQA (148 / 320), TAT-QA (362 / 4,754), TabFact (15,106 / 34,351)
limitations: Stated: text-only serialized tables, so tables embedded in scans, PDFs, spreadsheets or images are out of scope; the reasoning traces come from one teacher (DeepSeek-R1) and may carry its biases and artifacts; English-only benchmarks limited to QA and fact checking. Beyond those, the headline percentage gains are all relative to an unfine-tuned base model, so they conflate the benefit of reasoning conditioning with the benefit of any fine-tuning at all; the isolated contribution of conditioning over generation is the CoTCond-vs-CoTGen margin, which is a few points at most. The authors' own error analysis concedes that most of the gain is the suppression of malformed, empty and duplicate rankings rather than better ordering, which makes the result partly about output formatting robustness. Every number is a single run with no seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests, and SQA (148 queries) and TAT-QA (362 queries) are small. CoTCond requires a teacher trace in the prompt during training but the paper does not describe what conditioning context the trained model receives at test time, while still emitting 2,145-2,634 output tokens at inference, so the 'lower inference cost' claim is relative to CoTGen only and the model is not trace-free. The claimed multi-table generalization is asserted from the same aggregate tables rather than from a separate single- vs multi-table breakdown.
method: NQ-Tables training queries (9,574) are each given a candidate list built by reciprocal rank fusion over BM25, SPLADE-V3 and all-mpnet-base-v2, with 10-20 tables sampled per query and only samples retaining the gold table kept. DeepSeek-R1 is prompted with query plus candidate tables at temperature 0.7 and up to 8192 tokens, reasoning inside a <think> block before emitting a JSON ranking. Filtering (fewer than 9 candidates, over 25,000 tokens, incomplete generations, malformed or duplicated rankings) leaves 6,728 queries averaging 20.06 candidate tables and 2,304 reasoning tokens. Three students are trained from the same Qwen3-8B checkpoint with identical LoRA settings: Naive SFT, loss over the final ranking only with the trace discarded; CoTGen, standard distillation with loss over reasoning plus ranking tokens; and CoTCond, the proposed variant, where the input becomes x = [query; tables; teacher trace] and the loss is the autoregressive ranking loss conditioned on that trace, with no loss on reasoning tokens. The same prompt format covers single- and multi-table retrieval without architectural change, so a model trained only on single-table supervision can be evaluated on multi-table queries. Training used LLaMA-Factory, 2x H200 for about 18 hours, effective batch size 64, learning rate 5e-5.
methods: Reciprocal Rank Fusion over BM25, SPLADE-V3 and all-mpnet-base-v2
one_liner: TabRank distills DeepSeek-R1 reranking rationales into a Qwen3-8B listwise table reranker by placing the teacher's reasoning trace in the student's input prompt and computing loss only over the final ranking, rather than training the student to reproduce the trace.
problem: Multi-stage retrieval over structured data depends on a reranker to refine a first-stage candidate list, but reranking research has concentrated on unstructured passages, where relevance is largely lexical; table relevance also depends on column schemas, row alignment and inter-cell relations. Separately, the dominant way of adding reasoning to rerankers - training a student to autoregressively reproduce a teacher's chain of thought - has been reported to overfit dataset-specific reasoning trajectories and degrade cross-domain transfer, and to yield overly polarized relevance estimates. The paper asks how to get the benefit of teacher reasoning for table reranking without paying that cost.

relevance.overthinking: Tangential: this matched the topic only on the generic phrases 'large reasoning model' and 'reasoning trace'. The paper is about listwise reranking of tables for structured information retrieval, and its contribution is a distillation objective, not anything about how long a model should think or when it should stop. Two details are incidentally adjacent and worth noting only as such. First, the paper's central comparison is that not making the student reproduce the teacher's trace beats making it do so, at 12-35% fewer output tokens (e.g. 2,454 against 3,716 on TabFact) - a shorter-is-at-least-as-good result, but for a ranking objective under domain shift, with no accuracy/length curve and no per-instance length control. Second, the authors' own error analysis finds the gains come from eliminating malformed and duplicate rankings rather than from better ordering, and notes that CoTGen's long autoregressive chains 'increase opportunities for formatting drift' - which is a failure mode of long generation rather than of overthinking in the reasoning-budget sense. The one genuinely useful pointer for this topic is a citation, not a result: Jedidi et al. 2025, "Don't 'overthink' passage reranking: Is reasoning truly necessary?", which the archive does not appear to hold and which is on-topic in a way this paper is not.

results: All evaluation is out-of-distribution: training is NQ-Tables only, testing is on the HybridQA, SQA, TAT-QA and TabFact subsets of the Multi-Table QA Benchmark, reranking the top 25 first-stage tables. CoTCond is best on every dataset and metric reported. Accuracy@10 against the base Qwen3-8B: HybridQA 0.6200 -> 0.8091 (+30.5%), SQA 0.7095 -> 0.8176 (+15.2%), TAT-QA 0.3785 -> 0.4282 (+13.1%), TabFact 0.3816 -> 0.5835 (+52.9%). Against CoTGen rather than the base model the margins are much smaller: HybridQA Recall@5 0.7659 -> 0.7833 and Acc@10 0.7624 -> 0.8091, SQA Recall@10 0.8446 -> 0.8840, TAT-QA Recall@5 0.5124 -> 0.5520 and nDCG@10 0.5203 -> 0.5459, TabFact nDCG@10 0.6661 -> 0.6890 and Acc@10 0.5614 -> 0.5835. Naive SFT (no reasoning at all) is the weakest of the three fine-tuned variants and actually loses ground on TAT-QA ranking quality, nDCG@5 -1.2% and nDCG@10 -1.8% relative to base while recall rises. Mean output tokens at inference: CoTGen is longest everywhere (2983 HybridQA, 3318 SQA, 3704 TAT-QA, 3716 TabFact), CoTCond is 2634 / 2145 / 2473 / 2454 (12-35% fewer), and Naive SFT is cheapest at 1241-1365 but with the worst reliability. The error analysis is the load-bearing result: the base reranker's failures are dominated by structurally invalid output - duplicate predictions reach 16.8% on TabFact and 33.7% on TAT-QA, and the base model logs 489 failures on TabFact - and CoTCond cuts failures to 13 on HybridQA, 0 on SQA, 0 on TAT-QA and 45 on TabFact, with duplicates at 2.2% on TAT-QA and under 3% elsewhere. The authors state explicitly that the metric improvements 'stem from eliminating structural failures rather than from marginal reordering gains'. No variance or repeated-run statistics are reported for any number.
